newsitem.title: CONGO: Brazzaville talks run into obstacle but city calm.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville talks run into obstacle but city calm.

text.p: Plans to stage talks on ending fighting in the capital of the Congo Republic ran into a hurdle on Monday following objections from one of the warring parties.
But Brazzaville remained relatively calm, with only brief bursts of firing heard since mediators on Sunday called rivals to talks on Wednesday to halt the political conflict.

Supporters of Denis Sassou Nguesso, the opponent of President Pascal Lissouba in the conflict, accused the national mediation committee of jumping the gun on Sunday by issuing a statement on a ceasefire agreement.

"There is no signed agreement on a ceasefire -- there were only statements of intent on both sides," Francois Iboovi, a spokesman for Sassou, told Reuters. "It's difficult to talk about peace talks without such an agreement."

On Sunday the mediation committee said it was pleased to note the signing of a ceasefire agreement by parties to the month-long conflict. The committee called on both Sassou and Lissouba to participate in the planned round of peace talks.

Lissouba's spokesmen were not available to give the president's reaction to the committee's statement. Spokesmen for Bernard Kolelas, the head of the mediation committee, said they had no information on the reaction of either Lissouba or Sassou.

Kolelas, the city mayor, has met the two rivals separately in the past. Neighbouring Gabon's President Omar Bongo, a son-in-law of Sassou and friend of Lissouba, heads a separate international mediation effort.

The main bone of contention between Sassou and Lissouba remains the question of which authority should govern the former French Central African colony when Lissouba's presidential mandate expires at the end of August.

Lissouba says the constitution provides for his mandate to be prolonged for 90 days until elections -- which were scheduled for July 27 -- can take place. Sassou says the constitution makes no such provision and that a neutral transitional authority must take charge in the runup to elections.
The conflict between the two men has killed hundreds of people, displaced tens of thousands and devastated whole districts of Brazzaville.
Clashes broke out when government troops surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militias ahead of the elections.
In similar violence in 1993, at least 2,000 people were killed in Brazzaville after a disputed parliamentary election.
